question: Why does the 300 °C–300 °C multilayer urea crystal contain more nitrogen than the 300 °C single-layer crystal in the EDX results?
expect: premise false: it contains less nitrogen, 32.83 wt% against 35.15 wt% (more C and O), read as more cyanuric acid (Tables 9, 11; sec. 4.4)

- The elemental compositions of the multilayer urea crystal-lization samples were characterized by EDX, with the corresponding line-sum spectra presented in Figures 16−18 for the 300 °C−200 °C, 300 °C−300 °C, and 300 °C−400 °C samples, respectively.

- Given that the second-layer heating temperature was 300 °C—a temperature more favorable for CYA formation than for biuret—it is reasonable to conclude that the observed compositional change primarily reflects an increase in CYA content rather than biuret.

- Based on the collective results obtained from the three analytical techniques employed, it can be determined that: 1 The 300 °C−200 °C multilayer urea crystallization incorporates the chemical constituents present in the 300 °C single-layer urea crystallization, with the addi-tional formation of biuret. 2 The chemical composition of the 300 °C−300 °C multilayer urea crystallization differs from that of its 300 °C single-layer counterpart, primarily due to the formation of cyanuric acid (CYA) as an additional component. 3 The composition of the 300 °C−400 °C multilayer urea crystallization largely aligns with that of the 400 °C single-layer urea crystallization, possibly overlapping partially with the 300 °C single-layer composition, and likely incorporates melamine. 4 Compared to single-layer crystallization, the multilayer structure requires higher temperatures to achieve complete thermal decomposition, indicating enhanced thermal stability or the presence of decomposition barriers.
